subtopic: QUEBEC-RAIN MAKING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of any such negotiations. I have asked my Department to give me any information they had about these activities. As I said before in the House, the Department of Transport has had no connection with any rain making activities since 1963. I also asked the Vice President of the company that is engaged in these activities from Dorval-Weather Engineering, I think the firm is called-to come and see me last week. This gentleman assured me that no activity was being carried on by their company in the Lake St. John district at all. I asked him to put that in writing so I could communicate it to the House. maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a lew remarks to make in addition to my comments last night on the adjournment. I hope that the committee of the leaders of the various parties which is now meeting will come back very shortly and report success. I might say that the suggestion of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) indicates our anxiety and wish to get the business of the House moving.
Last night I said I supported the amendment made by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell). His amendment is to the effect that the motion that a Minister may make to allocate time would have to be approved by 60 per cent of the Members in the House. It is all very well to say that in a democracy the majority rules, but to me it is a perversion of democracy when a majority can close off debate by a substantial minority in any group. I might point out

that if all the Conservative Members of this House voted against such a motion by a Minister there would not be enough Members to defeat the motion. So even the approval of such motion by 60 per cent of the Members in the House is, in my opinion, a dangerous precedent, but it would at least offer a certain measure of safeguard for the protection of a very large minority. At the same time it would ensure that a very small minority could not delay indefinitely the decision of the House.
Last night I suggested to the Government a measure which they might consider to amend the guillotine proposal. My suggestion was that the allocation of time shall not become operative or effective until the bill or the matter under discussion had been referred to a standing or special committee of the House and such committee had reported back to the House. Since that time the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) has pointed out to me that this might raise a difficulty in that the matter would have to be referred to such committee before second reading had been given in the House. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, my suggestion now is slightly modified in that the limitation of time as to the committee stage, which is two days, and the limitation of time on third reading, which is one day as a minimum, shall not become operative or applicable unless the subject matter of the bill has been referred to a standing or special committee and such committee has reported back to the House. That would mean that the Government could apply a two day limitation on second reading, but the limitation at the committee stage and on third reading could not become effective until the standing or special committee of the House had reported.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
My proposal would overcome two objections. In the first place, as I now read clause 2, subclause 2 of Government Order No. 14, a Minister could move an allocation of time even before the Members of this House had seen a bill. As a matter of fact, as I read the wording of this subclause a Minister could move an allocation of time at any stage, perhaps even before a resolution appeared on the order paper.
In order to obviate that possibility, it seems to me that subclause 2 of clause 2 should at least refer to an item of business standing on the order paper; but even if that reference was made, a Minister, while not able to make a motion for the allocation of time unless the
June 8, 1965	COMMONS DEBATES	2103
subject matter had been placed on the order paper, could move such an allocation of time during the resolution stage. In other words, there could be an allocation of five days for a debate before any Member of the Opposition had an opportunity of seeing the bill. My suggestion would overcome that possibility. I realize that it is not very likely any Government in the future would so abuse the rules as to do that kind of thing, but the mere fact that it is possible should give concern to Members of this House.
The second effect of my proposal would be to overcome the objections of many Members who are afraid that at some time in the future a Government could rush a bill through this House without the opportunity for adequate scrutiny or investigation. If we are given the assurance that a standing or special committee of the House will have ample time to give thorough examination to a measure, then there would perhaps be some justification, though in my opinion not adequate justification, for a limitation of time on debate in the House following receipt of the report of that standing or special committee.
As I stated last evening, using the Canada Pension Plan, that complicated measure, as an example, under these rules it would be possible that the total amount of time available to this House for consideration of it, apart from the one day which is now allowed at the resolution stage, would be five days. Even if the standing or special committee had considered the question, the five day limitation would be possible, but at least there would be some assurance of an opportunity for thorough examination and scrutiny of a bill.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the objections raised by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mcllraith) about the 60 per cent amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell), I take it the Government will not accept my suggestion, but I do ask the Government to give it serious consideration because I feel that although it will not completely remove the danger of abuse by the use of the guillotine proposal, it would remove to some extent its adverse effects.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say at once that the remarks I am about to make would be considerably different, had the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) not accepted the suggestion I made in good faith in that same spirit.
House of Commons Procedures
I think during this debate Parliament has been most effective, but it would have been preferable, as has been stated, had we been able to consider this question in committee, so that in a community of discussion we would have been able to arrive at decisions in keeping with Parliament, and with the assurance that this great institution, now 700 years of age, would be carried on in the tradition of its greatness and its grandeur throughout succeeding generations, not only in Great Britain, but in the various parts of the Commonwealth that have followed the parliamentary system.
I say at once that the speeches that have been made have been unusually well prepared and thoroughly considered before delivery. An example of the type of speech we have heard is that of the hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Chatterton) who, in the suggestion he made today, exemplified the study he has made of this problem. What we have been trying to do is assure that parliament shall be effective without at the same time emasculating this institution. Naturally, there has been division of opinion. As I said a moment ago, it has been striking, in the comprehensiveness of the discussion that has taken place, that this debate has caused hon. Members generally in all parts of the House to make a study of parliament as an institution, for everywhere within the Commonwealth today there are criticisms of parliament, and there are many who claim that it does not operate with the effectiveness that it should operate. That criticism, however, has been answered over and over again. It was answered on one occasion by the greatest parliamentarian of our time, if not in all British history, and I refer to Sir Winston Churchill who set out in detail, on one occasion in the House of Commons, his conception of parliament and what it means.
Parliament is not measured by the number of statutes that are passed. Parliament is not a sausage machine into which is poured material by parliament and out of which, finally, after a couple of turns flows the output. It is nothing of the kind. Parliament is an institution which is effective, not in the amount of legislation it passes, but in the care and attention it gives to that legislation for the maintenance of freedom.
I criticize no one when I say that many of the speeches made by hon. Members, not on the front benches but the back benches, have not got through to the Canadian people. In
June 8. 1965

House of Commons Procedures other words, the people do not know the nature of the arguments that have been made. [DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
This is a serious matter. Hon. Members know that my attitude through the years has been that it would not be beneficial to parliament to broadcast, either by radio or television, a portion of each day's sitting. However, I am beginning to come to the point where I believe that this would be the course of reason, and the only way in which Canadians as a whole will be able to appreciate parliament, its mission, and the manner in which it discharges its responsibilities. This is a tremendous change in my thinking. It has come about because I believe that we will never make parliament effective by simply changing the rules. I think that is generally acceptable. I think of a speech delivered in this House by the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) in 1963. I had intended to refer to that in some detail, but I will do no more than say that he, as a parliamentarian who understands parliament, expressed it as his view that a mere change of the rules would not bring about efficiency or a change in the general attitude of parliament. With that, I agree.
I mentioned broadcasting a moment ago. In the Province of Saskatchewan when the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam-I always find it difficult to remember the constituency since I think only of the Member himself- was premier, they brought about radio broadcasts. I was not one who believed they would be beneficial. I think they have been. In Australia the matter is receiving consideration as to its continuance. The Australian radio industry is convinced that radio has made a comeback in the face of the challenge of television. The Prime Minister of Australia, Right Hon. Sir Robert Menzies, one of the great parliamentarians of the Commonwealth and a man who is cast in the mould of Churchill, Sheridan and Fox, has stated that radio broadcasting has not been beneficial in one particular, namely in the art of parliamentary debate. He believes that too often when Members are speaking with the radio before them during a broadcast, they forget the intimacy of the House of Commons and think only of the presence of their constituents far removed from parliament. However, I am coming to the conclusion that parliament can be made more effective if Canadians as a whole know more about it and its operations. I would welcome consideration by this House of broadcasting a portion of the daily sitting by radio, and also by television, provided it was in the

nature of an experiment. It is the only way I can see whereby young men and women in this House, new Members, can be projected to the people of Canada directly.
There is nothing more discouraging, and I have gone through it as a backbencher- there is no backbencher here who has not gone through it-than having prepared a most careful and thoughtful speech, and then find no reference to it in the press. Naturally, being human, one looks the next day in the press to determine the degree to which it has made an impact, only to find there is no reference whatever to the speech. I repeat what I have said on other occasions. Some elements of the press, and I think of the Toronto Globe and Mail, have gone a considerable distance toward providing a picture of parliament. However, no newspaper in our country has begun to approach the daily reports in the London Times which make parliament live. No one objects if there is a reference to his speech, but there is nothing more discouraging to the young Member of Pariament, and to the older ones who are backbenchers, than having burned the midnight oil only to find there is no reference to anything he said during the course of his speech. It is because of that I am turning more and more to the need of parliament to give consideration to allowing other media the privileges that they receive in other countries. I should like to see how it would work out. This is what we are here for to make this institution live.
During the last few weeks I have been reading, particularly and in detail, about the period from 1200 to 1350, the beginnings of Parliament as they were undertaken within a country in the British tradition. Throughout the years I have studied parliament. No one can be effective unless he understands the great history of this institution. At all times we, as parliamentarians, must guard against shortcuts, guard against the god of efficiency which from time to time raises its head in this institution. Shortcuts too often deny freedom. William Pitt summed up the situation, and I know the Prime Minister agrees because in his opening speech he dealt in a most philosophical way with the problem of parliament. Pitt said:
Necessity is the plea for every infringement of human freedom: it is the argument of the tyrant; it is the creed of slaves.
* (4:00 p.m.)
That is why we in Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition have been most carefully examining the suggestions made by the Government. We have not done so in a partisan
June 8, 1965

way. Sometimes I read that I am opposed to changes in Parliament. Nothing of the kind, Mr. Speaker. But I do not want changes made for the sake of change or for shortcuts the bureaucrats want; rather, I want changes that will maintain the mission and the greatness of this institution.
I want to thank the Prime Minister for answering the argument that I am a reactionary in this regard. In fact I can do no better than quote his words, as recorded at page 1480 of Hansard for May 19, the opening day of this debate, when he referred to extending the time of the House by working during the dinner hour:
I must acknowledge again, Mr. Speaker, that this important proposal to increase the sitting time of the House was suggested by the Leader of the Opposition.
Next he went on to quote my words in this regard and stated that his purpose in pointing out three suggestions that the Government had accepted was that he was trying to be very non-partisan and to associate the Leader of the Opposition with these proposals in order to acknowledge his paternity for some of them. Well, this is one kind of putative paternity that I have no objection to having ascribed to me, and I want to thank the Prime Minister for speaking in such authoritative tones.
Then he went on to quote my words as follows:
As far as questions are concerned, it is not for me to suggest, but I think that the number of these questions could be greatly reduced: and if we were also to have a self-denying ordinance that, under ordinary circumstances, we would not go over half an hour on questions before orders of the day we would save 15 full days in an ordinary session without, as I see it, losing any ground that might be gained through questions or in any way interfering with the rights of the Opposition.
These are changes I want to see made. So far as the question period is concerned, we are not always consistent in our views and I would hope the Prime Minister, in that spirit of co-operation which was displayed today, would agree that on one day a week the question period should be extended to an hour.
The attitude taken by Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition has been to endeavour to bring about agreement. As I said today in the question that I asked and in the subsequent discussion between the Prime Minister and myself, we are in agreement with most of the ideas that are still on the order paper but we still take a strong stand against this new
House of Commons Procedures form of closure that masquerades under the guise of being an allocation of time.
But I say to the Prime Minister that, as a result of parliamentary discussion and the spirit of give and take, the degree to which we have been able to agree has been quite amazing. The attitude of the Prime Minister in this regard has fully exemplified the responsibilities of his position and I, as the other officer of Parliament, have tried to reciprocate equally the spirit of give and take to the end that through discussion we will preserve this institution while extending and expanding its effectiveness.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: So far as the question period is concerned, I have said and I repeat that if we get answers to the questions on the order paper without having to wait weeks and months many of the questions that today are advanced as of immediate moment would not be asked, and if the answers given are straightforward answers much time would be saved. I am thinking of a recent example to which I intend to make extended reference later. Recently I asked the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) whether in effect the Government is contemplating changing the social security card to remove the Coat of Arms with its Crown, unicorn and the like and substitute a maple leaf. After a great deal of difficulty I was finally able to secure an answer that while the Government had not made a decision the matter was being looked into. Parliament has a right to say whether or not that change should be made. It should not be made behind closed doors just because there are some people who object to the Crown within this country.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
This is a matter that should not be decided by the desires or predilections of people who are forever casting aspersions on our British connection. The answer that was given had to be pried out, which should not be necessary.
Another thing I want to mention is something that is becoming almost a disease. Whenever we ask for the production of papers and it would be embarrassing to the Government to produce them, immediately there is recourse to the formula, "Let us transfer this for debate". This formula has been used throughout the years but it is simply a subterfuge to deny Parliament information, or to prevent the public knowing that what has
June 8, 196S

House of Commons Procedures been asked for has been denied by vote of the House.
As I said a moment ago, we must realize that Parliament is subject to criticism. Sometimes people tell me how different it is in the British House of Commons. I am going to add to the examples I gave in my earlier remarks to show that these things happen over there too. As recently as May 27 it was reported that the previous day, when a member was speaking in the British House, Mr. Speaker finally said:
There must be less noise. Members should remember the great privilege of being here and therefore allowed to listen to arguments with which they do not agree, e (4:10 p.m.)
There is not a week goes by that there are not articles on this subject. The Observer of May 2 carried an article entitled "Poor Old Parliament". Parliament is criticized, it says. Parliament must be renewed. Other institutions cannot be modernized if facilities for criticizing and planning are not modernized. As a reason why Parliament is not working the writer says that too much has been taken out of politics; in other words, too much has been given to bureaucrats to determine. I think there should be a full study made in Parliament of the whole problem of bureaucracy.
As I said a moment ago, we are not here to turn out legislation; we are here to preserve freedom. The other day we had an example. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) was asked a question a week ago Friday by the hon. Member for York-Hum-ber (Mr. Cowan). He was asked whether he would consider terminating a practice which has existed for hundreds of years by providing that the names of accused persons should not be mentioned during trial before conviction. All over this country a howl went up. I was shocked by the suggestion. I asked about the matter immediately. Then on Monday the Prime Minister found it necessary, because of the tremendous feeling that had been aroused in all parts of the country, to rise and say in effect that the Minister of Justice had not said at all what he had said, that if he had said what he had said he did not mean it, and if he did mean it the Government did not intend to act on it. This shows the power of publicity. Every newspaper across this country with, I think, one exception took the stand which I had taken, namely, that to follow the course suggested would be a denial of freedom. That is the purpose of Parliament, to preserve freedom.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext: May I put a short question to the right hon. gentleman? I understand that the Leader of the Opposition is not inferring that I suggested that course?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR CONSIDERATION OF ESTIMATES AND ALLOCATION OF TIME
speechtext:
No. The suggestion came from the hon. Member for York-Humber and the Minister, without thinking, I am sure, fell into an answer which was anything but appropriate. No, he did not make the suggestion at all. Let that be clear. But it was only as a result of publicity that this announcement found its way into the limbo of forgotten things. In other words, Parliament is freedom's cathedral. I will quote what Churchill said in this regard.
This House is not only a machine for legislation, it is a great forum of debate, and the process of legislation is not necessarily smooth because it is rapid or violent. The House ought to have the opportunity of moulding and shaping the laws which afterwards have to be obeyed by the people. The people give their obedience to the laws of this country to an extent remarkable, almost renowned. The people are renowned for their obedience to law, but that is because the law comes to them from a Parliament which they themselves have chosen, and because it is believed that all views have had a fair chance of expression in that Parliament, that the minority as well as the majority have been able to put their hand upon the legislative proposals. While the Government of the day naturally carry their own program, the legislation which emerges from our discussions is not simply party legislation, but legislation which bears the stamp of Parliamentary influence.
Also, the House has a function not merely of passing the bills, but of stopping bad bills from passing.
I emphasize that very strongly. It often takes several days discussion before we begin to realize the great weakness of some of the legislation which is introduced. This was the attitude taken by Sir Winston in 1945. He said:
I am most anxious that that process of general discussion should be widened. If the House is not able to discuss matters which the country is discussing, which fill all the newspapers, which every one is anxious and preoccupied about, it loses its contact, it is no longer marching step by step with all the thought that is in progress in the country. Therefore, we should save as much time as we can from routine matters, for the purpose of enabling large debates to take place.
I have strong objection to this allocation of time proposal, this limitation to be imposed by the Government after there has been disagreement in the committee. Take a proposition such as this as an example. We always choose something that is striking when we are looking for an example. Suppose this Government were to decide that Canada was to become a republic and suppose it had in the second Chamber appointees
June 8, 1965

who were of the same view. Even though many of us stood against it, the proposition could be put through in a maximum of three days if these rules were in effect.

speechtext: Six days.

speechtext:
It may save time if we pass rules which would bring about the throttling of Parliament in this way but they should certainly not be applied in order to prevent debates on great subjects of national interest.
I can point out another example, and I shall not enter into detail. It is in connection with a measure now before the Government, according to information from the press. It concerns an Address from the legislature of Quebec which it has been requested be transmitted to Her Majesty the Queen. It is an Address which would trim the wings of the second Chamber, the legislative Council of Quebec. I am not arguing the question whether or not there should be a second Chamber. The constitution provides that the Legislature of Quebec consists of the Queen, the Legislative Council and the Legislative Assembly. Apparently as far back as February Mr. Lesage, according to what he says, was anxious to have an agreement with the Federal Government that whatever Address might be passed by the Legislature would be forwarded to the Queen with a recommendation of acceptance by the Government of Canada.
I say to you, Sir, that this is something that should be debated in this House. How can the Government of Canada maintain that the Legislature of Quebec, which alone has the power to amend the Constitution in so far as Quebec is concerned, does not, as the British North America Act says, consist of the Queen, the Legislative Council and the Legislative Assembly? How can the Government of Canada, whatever undertakings or promises it may have given to Mr. Lesage, circumvent the Constitution and place Her Majesty in the centre of political controversy? [DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
That is something that should be guarded against. It is because of this that I say to the Prime Minister-I am not going to argue the case at the moment; I hope the opportunity will come in a day or so-that to pass on that Address from the Legislative Assembly of Quebec to amend the Constitution of Quebec is, in the face of the British North America Act, a course that cannot but bring Her Majesty into the political arena and it is 22620-135

House of Commons Procedures one that is not in keeping with the responsibilities of the Government of Canada.
This is something that deserves to be discussed here, for certainly if you accept that proposition we could abolish the Senate or trim its powers by a simple vote of the House of Commons of Canada, with the Government of Canada through its Prime Minister advising the Queen that an amendment to the Constitution should take place in the United Kingdom. It is dangerous doctrine to say that you are going to accept the viewpoint of one-third of the elements of the Legislature of Quebec. To do so will go contrary to every principle in this regard. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, when one looks at the discussions that took place in 1868 when Nova Scotia decided that it wanted to secede or in 1898 when the Legislative Assembly of Nova Scotia decided to trim the powers of the Legislative Council which Nova Scotia had at that time, it will be seen that the authorities in London said, "This course we will not accept", while not going into particulars as to the reason for the non-acceptance. Let me point out, however, that when the Legislative Council of Nova Scotia was finally abolished in 1928, I think it was, both Houses joined in the Address. Then, of course, the Address could be passed on to the Sovereign as representing the viewpoint of that Province.
This is a question that cannot be laughed off. If we in this Parliament condone the action of the Government in carrying out a promise which the Premier of Quebec says he got in writing on March 11, namely, that whatever Address was passed by the Legislative Assembly would be passed on to the Sovereign with the recommendation of the Government, then we will have struck a tremendous blow at the Constitution. We know what the reason is for this; it is because Premier Lesage has stated that if they wait until the amendment of the Constitution goes through-the Fulton-Favreau formula-they will never be able to trim the wings of the Legislative Council. This is a matter deserving of the consideration of this Parliament, for to accept the proposition now advanced would be indeed to strike a body blow at the sacrosanct nature of the British North America Act.
There is one other matter that ought to be referred to and that is the question of the Speakership. I was not the one who suggested a permanent Speaker, although some have asked me what I mean by a "permanent Speaker". I borrowed the word "permanent" from the Prime Minister. It was he who
June 8. 1965

House of Covimons Procedures raised this question in his original speech; he said that the question of a Speaker having permanency was of importance. I followed in using the expression and advocated the need of this being done. I press it again. I am not being provocative at the moment but we have had the experience of a Speaker who became the puppet and the robot of the Government in power in 1956 and we are afraid to place in the hands of a non-independent Speaker the exercise of the powers that are inherent in the limitation of time for discussion principle. That is why I think we should not run away from the question of a permanent Speaker.
I suggested His Honour who today occupies the Chair. There will be the start. How would we do it? Well, Mr. Speaker, we cannot bind subsequent Parliaments but we can make a gentlemen's agreement as they do in the United Kingdom. I notice that Your Honour, who is occupying the Chair temporarily, points to yourself. If it were not for your innate modesty I might join you in the company of those who might be recommended.

speechtext: We have a Speaker. From what has been said he is universally honoured in this House. Is this not the time to start along this course? The Prime Minister mentioned his alternatives, one of whom was Hon. Roland Michener. He is not here-

He eliminated himself in a speech in Cornwall in which he said he did not want anything to do with being a permanent Speaker whom he interpreted to be a kind of permanent civil servant. There was no such suggestion at any time, but he eliminated himself as not being interested. I come back to this, that if we want to make this House effective let us start by having a permanent Speaker.
I mentioned a moment ago that the Prime Minister himself had used that expression and I am sure he recalls having done so when he first brought the matter before the House. Let us do the job. Let the committee composed of the various House leaders make this recommendation. Then we would be in a position to know whether or not His Honour would accept. Up to the present time he has given no indication. And that is proper; he should not give any indication. A

Speaker does not ask for the appointment; indeed, the whole essence of the appointment of a Speaker is that he does not want it. That is why when finally the House accepts his name we push him into the Chair. We do so because there was a time, Mr. Speaker, when occupying the Chair was not one of those positions that was universally desired, for too often the paths of glory led but to the grave. This is the reason. I come back to this, Mr. Speaker, and say that I hope the Government will act in this regard. Do not let us postpone this question. We are all in agreement at the moment on the need of this being done. Let us not pass it off until after the next election.
There are other questions I might have dealt with but what I rose to do today was simply this. I rose to repeat our desire, to repeat my desire, that we make this an effective House. The hon. Member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said that the matter should not be discussed. I have quite an admiration for the duality of his capacity from day to day. He sits on Mount Olympus and in the press determines the relative position, capacity and ability of every Member of this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I say to the hon. gentleman that it is given to few of us to be so high that we can look down on others and point out their weaknesses and then determine their qualifications by numbers. So far as other Members of the House are concerned, we receive daily treatment in this regard. No other Member of the press can do it because there is none so close to us. The others look down to us from above; he is on our level. Therefore he is able to speak with that detachment which comes from knowledge and wisdom. He took the view that we should not be discussing this question but that view was not generally held, and I think rightly so.
I hope we will be able to bring about agreement, the signs of which have been so apparent during the entire discussions that have taken place here. But do not think that these changes are going to bring about the millenium. I again repeat what the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) said in 1963, that changing the rules will not do it and that reducing the period of time in which each member speaks will not do it. It is a difficult Parliament with a multitude of parties, and with several of them endeavouring to be
June 8, 19G5

placed on an equality with Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition it is difficult to bring about agreement. Are we going to be more effective? I hope so. Some of these changes will be tremendously beneficial. They were born with the midwives from all parts of the House making their contribution.
As to the change respecting which there is disagreement, I hope that a committee of House Leaders or a Committee of the House will be able to go into the matter more fully than we can and that, they can come up with an alternative that will assure the preservation of the right of Members to express themselves on great issues and not to be placed in hobbles whenever the Government fears that discussion may be weakening to the position it has taken.
So far as examination of estimates in Committee is concerned, I can only say that no one can tell me that we are going to be able to discharge in 36 days the major responsibility we have of preserving and maintaining the financial responsibility of the Government. In looking into the estimates of this country we would have to examine them at a rate of $50 million an hour. We are not expected to look at the general picture but what we are expected to do is to look into those items which we believe deserve examination. In following what has been the experience in the United Kingdom we do not cover the whole ambit, as it were, and thereby dissipate our energies on unnecessary words or fatuous examination.
I conclude, Sir, by expressing my appreciation of the attitude taken by the Government in accepting various amendments or ideas advanced by the Opposition. That is the proper spirit in which to act, not by threatening an election every now and then in order to browbeat and bulldoze. We should act in a spirit of endeavouring to come to an agreement, not for this side of the House or for that side of the House but for Canada. That has been the attitude in general.
I could have made a very different speech today had not the Prime Minister shown this attitude, and it is in the same spirit that I have spoken. This place is the only location where freedom is maintained, conserved and assured, and we want to preserve that freedom by maintaining the greatness of those things of the past while at the same time making the changes which are necessary in order to assure that the institution shall not perish because of our failure to go forward with the times. However, we must at the same time demand that the changes shall 22620-1355
House of Commons Procedures be made not by way of experiment as to what may happen but based on experience as to what does happen and has happened in various countries of the world, because in some, as a result of alterations in the rules, parliamentary institutions have simply become the instrument to turn out what the Government then in power desires and demands.

I anticipate being in London next week and I notice that in the proposals for the Prime Ministers' Conference- these are off and not on the agenda-[DOT] there are two ceremonies which have very real significance to this Parliament. At Westminster Hall, which is the very cradle of the Parliamentary system, at the Guildhall, which has also made its contribution to that system, there will be a commemoration of the 700th anniversary of Parliament. This is an interesting indication of the depth of our Parliamentary roots and the importance of our Parliamentary traditions today, as well as their value in these times of change in the world, change which is not always peaceful. It is also an indication of the importance of preserving and strengthening our Parliamentary roots and traditions and those functions which we have been discussing, and the value of maintaining and strengthening our Parliamentary rights.
The hon. gentleman said, and I paraphrase his remarks I hope correctly, that it is not primarily our responsibility to work here to turn out legislation but to preserve freedom. Undoubtedly it is a major responsibility of Parliament to preserve freedom, freedom of our democratic institutions and freedom of individuals whom we represent. When the right hon. gentleman talked about the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau), and I am not complaining about what he said for one moment, let me state that the Minister of Justice had in mind the reconciliation of one freedom with the other, the freedom of the press as an institution with the freedom of the individual.

our work and responsibility to preserve freedom, but it is also our responsibility to pass legislation, to make proposals and to put them into operation. Somehow Parliament has to reconcile these things, its function as the preserver of freedom and its function as the producer of legislation, in a way which will make the freedom of our country and the freedom of the individual effective in terms of the day in which we live.
What we are attempting by the proposals before us dealing with procedure and rules is to make Parliament more effective in its legislative function without prejudicing in any way its responsibility to preserve other freedoms through discussion in this House; and discussion is the basis of freedom. That is what we have in mind on all sides of the House in the discussions we have been having as to how to preserve and strengthen Parliament and how to provide for adequate and effective decision. That is what we have had in mind when we have been discussing provision for talk, and for relating that talk eventually to action; and how to adapt our procedure to the action required by changing needs and changing circumstances.
We have often reminded ourselves in this House that 50 years ago the problem of the Government was to find enough legislation to keep Members here for two or three months. Sir John A. Macdonald often worried about how to get enough work to do so he would be here for six weeks. This is a problem that does not seem to worry me very much at the present time.

That was a very special situation, but normally it was not a full time occupation. Governments did not have to worry too much about the time required to get their legislative programs through. This certainly is a major preoccupation for any Government now, to get time in Parliament to deal with the things that should be done.
In this House, Mr. Speaker, we are asked on this side, as we should be asked: When are you going to do this? When are you going to bring in that? What is your policy on this? It is a major problem now to reconcile full and free discussion with the necessity for quick and effective action in respect of at least some major matters that should come before this House. I agree with my right hon. friend and with others who have spoken in
DEBATES	2111
House of Commons Procedures this debate that we are not going to make Parliament effective necessarily by changing the rules. That will not be enough. It is the spirit behind the rules that is more important than the rules themselves. No matter how much we may change the rules in the hope that they will make Parliament more effective, there will always be those, if they have the desire, who can use the rules for purposes which others will call blocking and delaying.
While new rules themselves will not be enough, out of date rules will certainly make it far more difficult for us to do the things we want to do. We do have an obligation to try to bring our rules into line with the needs and requirements of the times. This is what is behind these two resolutions. My right hon. friend talks about the importance of strengthening the prestige and position of Parliament in the public mind. Of course this is important. I think that we, as Parliamentarians, do have a kind of trade union feeling amongst ourselves when we face the world. We all agree that something should be done in this connection to improve the position-I believe the jargon is the image-of Parliament. How fine it would be if we could get what we consider to be the right kind of reflection of what we are trying to do here, in the press, radio and television.
It is natural that our activities will get the most publicity when they can be interpreted in terms of excitement and conflict. This applies to every institution of which I have any knowledge, national or international. Go down to the United Nations Assembly and you will find you will get more publicity if you make a speech which is interpreted in terms of conflict, especially in terms of cold war conflict. It will get the headlines. Down the hall there may be a committee which is dealing with Viet Nam or Santo Domingo and it will have all the newspapermen, radio men and television men cluttered around giving that committee all the publicity they can. Another committee may be discussing ways of getting more grain to grow in Afghanistan, which will mean the difference between life and death for a lot of people, and there will be no publicity given to it. So, this must be our fate in this House when we are making these learned, quiet, constructive speeches. We do not get as much publicity as if we got into a row with people on the other side.
I do not know what we can do about this except, perhaps, as the hon. gentleman said, to consider an experiment in televising our proceedings. I was interested in his observa-

speechtext:
I am grateful to the House for its consideration and I will try not to presume on its kindness.
The changes we are proposing in the rules and procedures are, of course, only a means to an end. As I have said, the end is the more effective conduct of our business, the effective functioning of our system. These proposed changes, Mr. Speaker, are not new. As I said when I spoke before in this debate, they represent about 15 months of very hard allparty work. Most of the proposals were proposals that came from the work of that allparty committee. These proposals were embodied in two resolutions and put before the House because the Government felt it was its duty to take that responsibility. I said at the time they were not put forward in any take it or leave it manner. I think our conduct since that time has justified that statement on my part because the Government has accepted a great many changes to the proposals that have been submitted. These changes, I think, certainly have improved the original resolution. They have managed to get a wider basis of support for the changes and that is very important when we are dealing with Parliamentary institutions.
Perhaps I could just put the changes on the record. They are, removing supplementary estimates introduced after main estimates have been approved and final supplementaries from the order for allocation of time; remov-
June 8. 1985

ing supply motions and lengthening the time for discussion of estimates; supply motions to be reduced from six to four and the days for supply to be increased from 36 to 38. No allocation of time by a Minister's motion can be less than two days for second reading, two days for committee stage and one day for third reading. That is a very important change proposed from the other side of the House, which insists that in any time allocation there will be substantial time for debate, whatever the proposal may be. A provision has been put in that each party must have the right to speak on any stage under any allocation of time.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
We have provided that after an amendment the Speaker may extend the time allocated up to two days, that is, if an amendment is made during a debate which introduces something of importance into the resolution there shall be additional time given for its discussion. Further, Mr. Speaker, the motion provides that allocation of time, whenever used, may include fixing of limits for length of speeches. Most important-I am talking now only about allocation of time-this order shall be on a trial basis only.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, this gives us the right to say that we have approached this matter in as non-partisan a manner as is possible. The proposals we have now before us are ones which I think meet the wishes of the majority of the Members of the House.
The right hon. gentleman objects strenuously to one aspect of these proposals which has been referred to as the guillotine but which we call the allocation of time for debate. This, of course, is the very heart of our proposals for making our House of Commons more effective in the dispatch of legislative proposals. Surely when the safeguards which I have mentioned and others are included in the proposals, it is exaggeration to call this aspect of them a guillotine or a new form of closure.
I do not wish at this time to go into the resolution itself to show how carefully guarded these proposals are to ensure that the Government will not have its own way automatically and that there will be no possibility of gagging backbenchers on either side of the House, to ensure that there are restrictions around the exercise of authority by the Government, to ensure that whatever business is to be done by the Business Committee will be done through unanimity and
House of Commons Procedures not by Government action, because it is the Business Committee which will try to agree on this time allocation on request by the Government. In that committee the Government representative will be only one of five Members, and if there cannot be agreement in the committee then the matter can be brought forward in the House by the Government through a proposal which is to be carefully restricted along the lines I have indicated and the changes I have just read.
Surely it is not right to consider these proposals as weakening or destroying Parliamentary debate or as a form of closure which would gag the House of Commons. This is the kind of thing which is done regularly in Parliament at Westminster and which has been found almost an indispensable part of the procedure there. It is not done in the same way but the principle of time allocation is in effect in the Parliament at Westminster.

speechtext:
It is the same principle which is embodied in these proposals and I suggest that this principle, if it is put into operation by a decision of the House, will not weaken but strengthen Parliament, will not remove from this House full freedom of discussion but will ensure that after that discussion has taken place, within a reasonable time by agreement or by decision of the House if agreement cannot be reached, there will be a decision made on the matter under discussion. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, this is a most effective way to strengthen, not weaken, parliamentary institutions and in strengthening parliamentary institutions to increase the prestige and the position of the House of Commons and to strengthen the position of individual Members in the House. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this is something that is worth doing.
I suggest, now that we have had a good many days of debate, by agreement among the House Leaders-they have been discussing this matter this afternoon-and along the lines I have suggested we will be able in a day or two to come to a decision in respect of all matters within these proposals whether or not the proposals be divided.
I feel quite certain, if anything is certain in this world, that if these proposals are put into operation the result will be that at the end of the first full session of the House of Commons, when under these proposals we are obligated to reconsider and re-examine

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Grant Wahn (St. Paul's) moved
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-7, respecting Interprovincial Pipe Line Company.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to divide each of the 40,000,000 authorized shares of the par value of $5 each of the capital stock of the company into five shares of the par value of $1 each. This bill was before the House briefly during the last session. Questions were raised as to the purpose of the stock split and as a result of those questions a great deal of research has been done with regard to stock splits. This research has proved to be valuable and I think it will be most interesting to Members of the House and to Members of the Committee to which I assume the bill will be referred in due course.
Perhaps I could refer briefly to the history of the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company in order that Members may be familiar with it. The Company operates strictly as a common carrier under the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board of Canada. It transports oil, not gas. It neither buys nor sells any oil. It is similar to a railway in this respect; it is purely a transportation undertaking and it carries all the oil tendered to it under published tariffs. As I mentioned, the Company and its undertakings are subject to the jurisdiction of the National Energy Board of Canada which has the power to regulate the rates charged. I may add that the National Energy Board is aware of this application to Parliament and has no objection to the stock split. It is proposed that a representative of the National Energy Board be invited to the Committee to which this bill will be referred and he will be available there for examination should Members consider this to be desirable.
Over a period of years the company has gradually developed what is believed to be
June 8. 1965

the longest oil pipe line in the world and since it first commenced operations it has steadily reduced the rate per barrel charged for the transportation of oil, the total reduction amounting to about 42 per cent. It is believed the rate charged by the Company for the transportation of oil is the lowest per mile charged by any oil pipe line company in the world.
The officials and directors of the Company, the management, are all Canadian. I have their names should any Members be interested. The shareholders also are largely Canadian. The figures I have reflect the position as of December 31, 1964. At that time approximately 88 per cent of the outstanding shares were owned by Canadian individuals or companies, 11 per cent in the United States and 1 per cent elsewhere. In fairness I should say that included in those figures for Canadian ownership are shares owned by such Canadian companies as Imperial Oil, British American Oil and Shell of Canada Limited, which in their turn have the majority of their shares owned outside Canada. Nevertheless, the Company is in its management and in the nature of its operations essentially a Canadian Company. It is also a fact that it is a Company very highly regarded throughout Canada and by the investment community.
I come now to the reasons for the stock split. It is believed that if the stock is split in the manner suggested the effect would be to increase the number of individual Canadian shareholders. Questions were raised with regard to this point when the bill was last before the House and as a result, as I have mentioned, some extensive research was done to establish the truth of this statement. A well known investment Company has made a complete review of stock splits in recent years in Canada and the United States. It has concluded that after a stock split without exception there has been an increase in the number of shareholders far greater than in the case of companies which have high priced shares and do not split their stock.
In the case of Interprovincial the price of the stock on the markets is approximately $90 a share and this is regarded as a very high price stock. It has also been established by the study I have mentioned that when the price of a stock reaches the $80 to $100 range it becomes impracticable for investors to buy or sell small numbers of shares at advantageous prices. Accordingly it is not economical for small investors to invest in stock which
Private Bills
sells at the price of Interprovincial stock at the present time. The study to which I have referred indicates that Canadian investors have a preference for shares selling at between $10 and $25. The evidence on this point is conclusive. Perhaps I might take a few seconds in which to mention it.
No less than 41.7 per cent of the shares traded on the Toronto stock exchange fall within this price range. An analysis of stocks traded during the whole of 1964 shows that 42.7 per cent of the total volume were within this range, $10 to $25. This high percentage of trading activity means there is a narrow margin between the bid price and the asked price with the result that price movements are less erratic and small investors may buy or sell shares without sacrifice. The study concludes that the marketability of stock is, without question, greater when the price falls within the range I have mentioned.
I feel the desirability of the split can be conclusively established. Perhaps the question then arises: Why should the stock be split in this particular ratio, five for one? The reason is that, as indicated, the shares would then be worth between $10 and $25 and would be within the most marketable range. A five for one split of Interprovincial stock would reduce the price to around $18 and this seems to be by far the most desirable split. Not only would it bring the price range into the area of maximum marketability but it would mean that shareholders who now own shares would own multiples of five shares. This works to the advantage of individual investors because stock market practice is for holdings of multiples of five to be by far the most frequently traded. For this reason they can be traded most cheaply.
However, following the debate in the House last session the company did review the effect of a smaller split, say three for one or two for one. This would result in a higher price per share and would reduce the marketability of the shares. The possibility of a larger split was also considered. A split of ten for one, for example, would reduce the price to $9, and a split of 20 for one would reduce the price below $5. The study indicated that this would attract speculation in the stock rather than investment. There would be people who would buy the stock simply because it was cheap, and this would not be in the interests of the investor or for that matter in the interests of the company.

The study indicated that this is true not only in Canada but also in the United States where the question ol stock splits was considered by the New York Stock Exchange. In particular, the New York Stock Exchange considered the ratio in which stocks should be split. I should like to quote the views of the New York Stock Exchange as contained in the following paragraph:
A split-up of a stock already selling in a low price range and a split-up which may result in an abnormally low price range for the split-up shares will be carefully scrutinized by the Exchange.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the New York Stock Exchange feels that care should be taken not to split a stock too far. For these reasons it was felt that the five for one stock split proposed in this bill was just about right. I might also mention that this particular stock split has been approved by the directors of Interprovincial Pipe Line Company and has also been approved by the shareholders. In addition, it has been very strongly supported by the employees of the company who belong to the employees' savings plan which the company has established. Under that savings plan employees can save in cash or they can authorize their savings to be invested in stock, including stock of the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company.
Following the debate in the House last session a questionnaire was sent to all the employees who participated in the company plan to see what their views were with regard to the stock split. Very careful precautions were taken so that employees could answer the questionnaire without divulging their names. The first question put to the employees was this:
Would it be more attractive to you as an avenue of investment of your Plan savings if the stock were subdivided on a 5 for 1 basis, so that each new share would have a market value of approximately $18?
The answer to that question was 90 per cent "Yes". The second question was:
If you presently allocate your Plan savings to cash savings, or are contemplating doing so some time in the future-
Rather than authorizing investment in stock.
-would the lower unit price of the Company stock encourage you to change your allocation from cash savings to the purchase of Company stock?
The answer to that question was 78.7 per cent "Yes". There is very wide participation of employees in the employees' savings plan and there was a very wide participation of employees in answering the questionnaire. I

believe that Interprovincial has just under 600 employees. The total number of employees polled was 561 and the total number of replies received was 508.
To summarize very briefly what I have said, Mr. Speaker, it would appear that the stock split is in the interests of the shareholders of the company and in the interests of the public generally in that it will help to distribute these shares more widely across Canada, and it has been approved by the directors, shareholders and employees of the company. There seems to be no objection to it on the grounds of public policy, and for these reasons I hope this bill will secure the support of the Members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill No. S-7 because it permits an opportunity to bring to the attention of the House and the people certain facts embedded in this question which the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) has not taken the trouble to explain and also the officials of Interprovincial Pipe Line Company have not taken the trouble to explain, nor did they explain them when this bill was before the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines about three months ago on March 11, 1965.
In view of the relationship between the ownership pattern of these various companies and the prices they charge one may talk about any phase of the oil industry and still be on the beam in dealing with the basis of the great unrest among the people of my riding of Macleod and also throughout the whole of Alberta-I understand this is also true of other parts of Canada-with regard to the situation of constant, almost ever-increasing increases in gasoline prices. It has got to the point that people who wish to travel must think twice because of the cost of filling their automobile tanks with gasoline or of propelling their tractors and other farm equipment. These prices are going up continually.
There have been increased taxes.

Yes, there have been increased taxes. I believe an increase in tax was imposed by Alberta but was withdrawn a short time ago. I understand, too, that in Edmonton a committee has been appointed to investigate prices of gasoline and the problems of retailing it throughout the Province of Alberta. There is a tremendous amount of unrest among the dealers in this regard. They are

pretty much all tied up by Imperial Oil Company, the B.A. Oil Company and Shell. It is about these three corporations that I wish to say a few words because they are the real owners of the company that is under consideration here, Interprovincial Pipe Line Company, whose management is asking for authority to split the shares. According to the articles of incorporation the management must seek from Parliament authority for splitting the shares and this is what they are seeking to obtain.
What is the pattern of ownership of this corporation, Mr. Speaker? Let me not use my own words but those of the President of the corporation, Mr. Johnston, who said on March 11 last when he appeared before the committee:
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Yes, Sir. Imperial Oil, who were the instigators of the program back in 1949 own 33 per cent; B.A. (American) own about 8 per cent which is the stock which originally was sold to Gulf Oil, and Shell, who now own Canadian Oil, participates in the company to the extent of 100,000 shares. If you add those up it is 47 per cent.
That gives exactly the pattern of the major interests in Interprovincial Pipe Lines. So that the policy of the company is controlled by the major interests such as Imperial Oil, B.A. and Shell and it is therefore in a position to operate as a monopoly.
That is the reason why inserted into their articles of incorporation was the provision that they must come back to Parliament and ask Parliament if they can have a split in shares. This also provides Parliament with an opportunity to look at the policies of the company and at what the company has been charging for services and for transporting oil. We are provided with the opportunity of asking for information from this monopoly as to its services and charges and the policies it has been following to promote the oil industry and the economy of Canada in general.
Many things might be said in favour of this Corporation but I think some matters should be given further consideration and discussion. For example, let us consider the pattern of ownership which I have mentioned earlier. Take, for example, the ownership of the President of the Corporation, Mr. Johnston. As reported at page 875 of the proceedings before the Standing Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines on March 11, 1965, Mr. Johnston said:
I am perfectly honest about this: there is no ulterior motive in this. There is no intention on the
Private Bills
part of management or the directors to participate in any way in any extravagant bonanza, as you might call it, or anything else. If the stock is split, the price will be reduced accordingly. The dividend will be reduced accordingly. It really is as simple as that. I believe quite often people have a misconceived idea that a board of directors or large shareholders will participate in these stock splits to a large extent. I can indicate to you that I am the largest shareholder on the board of directors. I hold 3,637 shares of stock which is not an extravagant amount.
The President of the Corporation has there put on the line the number of his shares, and I must add that that number is no greater and in some cases probably less than presidents of corporations sometimes own. But in this case there is a vast difference. In this case he is directing a Company that is in a position to exercise monopoly control over the charges it makes for the services it renders.
Let me pursue this matter a little further. There are 5,087,282 shares of this Corporation outstanding. Of that amount 3,166,501 shares can be accounted for as to ownership because it can be ascertained from various publications which have been issued. If you subtract one from the other you arrive at a figure of 1,920,781 shares which is the floating supply. Some of that floating supply is purchased and held on the way up by speculators who are waiting for a split to take place in order to unload their shares on the small people. That is one of the practices of speculators.
What usually happens following distribution, is that the stock declines and there are shake-outs. I am not saying that that is what the pattern of this stock is going to be but in general that is how the market works. Yet these people come here with tears in their eyes and the freshman from St. Paul's parrots what these people have said about splitting stock in order to get the small fry in. Who is going to benefit? These people now own the shares and they are the ones who will benefit, not the small fry they are sucking in. If they hold on to the shares from 5 to 15 years they may benefit eventually but they are certainly not the ones who are going to benefit immediately. It is the people who now own the shares who will benefit immediately.
Let me return to Mr. Johnston's holding of 3,637 shares. At $90 a share his holding is worth $327,330, which is a pretty fair equity in a corporation. What usually happens when stocks are split-the hon. Member for St. Paul's did not tell us this-is that

Company and others on the back and tell them that they have done a good job, but at the same time every Member of this House should believe, as the people of the area believe, that the prices for gasoline are to high and that somebody in a monopoly position is taking too much for the service being performed. If you believe that I do not know what I am talking about just pay a visit to my riding and it will not be long before you hear the people there repeating this same story which I am only parroting.
It is all well and good for the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company to suggest that it is not responsible for the fixing of prices because it does not own the oil, but the major owners of the company are setting gasoline prices, such as Imperial and Shell, but let me assure you that is not the complete picture. This brings me to another problem, namely, the regulatory body established for examining the practices of certain corporations. When we were in power we established the Energy Board and charged that body with the task of setting up the necessary machinery to conduct studies of the situation and recommend measures to protect the interests of the people and to confer with provincial authorities in this regard.
It is all well and good for the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) to suggest that this stock split has been sanctioned by the Energy Board, but I have not been made aware of the fact that it has been so sanctioned. That board certainly has made no public statement to that effect. I am in favour of the National Energy Board and I worked hard for the establishment of it, but let me say that when I made a study for the Gordon Royal Commission and put together "Alberta's Economic Prospects", working as an economic consultant for the Alberta Government and assisted by about 50 people from various Departments of the Government of Alberta, after three or four months we found-

Mr. Speaker, there have been a number of occasions in this House when we have had discussions involving the general principle set forth in this Bill, which is in fact a proposal to split the shares of the Interprovincial Pipe Line Company. Members of the New Democratic Party have made it clear on a number of occasions that we view these proposals, to put it mildly, with a jaundiced eye. Some of the reasons advanced for the splitting of shares are viewed by Members of this Party in that way.
From time to time we have presented documentation to this House in relation to the results of share splitting of this kind in the past. The explanatory note in the bill reads in part as follows:
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The reason for the proposed subdivision is that the company considers it desirable that the average Canadian investor be encouraged and be given the maximum opportunity and incentive to invest in the equity of a successful and growing Canadian company.
We certainly have some question in our minds when we find this bland assertion as to the real purpose the company has in coming before this House. However, we did have some considerable discussion of this matter during the last session when an almost identical bill to this one was before us. So far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to conclude my remarks at this time on the understanding this bill is going to committee for detailed study where we may have an opportunity to hear what the spokesmen for the company may say in answer to questions put by the Members of the committee.

Mr. Speaker, before the question is put I should like to pose a number of questions that are in my mind and were in my mind during the last time this bill was before the House and before the Committee. When the bill was before the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines I, along with a lot of other Members, posed some questions concerning the purpose of share splitting. I was interested in the remarks made by the hon. Member for St. Paul's (Mr. Wahn) when he discussed share splitting. He said that a 5 for 1 split was reasonable but that a 10 for 1 split or a 20 for 1 split might induce undue speculation in the company's shares. I was interested in this from the point of view that a 5 for 1 split would not do this but a 10 for 1 split would. I wondered how the hon. member could draw the line so closely.
It has been my belief that a stock split helps those who already hold shares. It is no surprise to me that the shareholders are in favour of a share split of 5 for 1. It is no surprise that the directors are in favour of this and no surprise that the company employees, who have an interest in their savings fund, should also be in favour of a share split.
The bill before us during the last session stated that the whole purpose of the proposal was to make it more desirable for the small Canadian investor to invest in this company. The explanatory note for this bill says that the proposal would make it more desirable for the average investor to invest in this company. During the Committee hearings last session I asked how many small investors had invested in this company already. The Chairman of the company who was before us at the time could not answer that question. I thought it rather strange that a company would come before Parliament or before the Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines Committee asking for a share split in order to encourage small investors when they did not know how many small investors they already had or how many they were trying to encourage into the company.
He went on to tell us that 47 per cent of the company stock was owned by Imperial Oil, Shell of Canada and British American. He said that the rest of the shares were owned by a number of people. In fact, he said that 37 people owned 10,000 shares or more. When I asked him, however, how many small investors had invested in the company he could not tell me. He said, as the hon. Member for

St. Paul's has, that share splitting has proven to be a factor in enticing greater participation in a company. Going back over the years as far back as 1958, we find this company had 12,000 shareholders. Surely the stock was not up around $90 at that time. Since that time the number of shareholders has only increased to 14,000. Evidence before the Committee in the last session suggested that the most recent investors in the company had been pension plans and funds similar to pension funds held by unions and other companies. This does not suggest to me that the average investor is being kept out of this company by the high price of the shares.
I suggest that before the company comes before the committee to give evidence they bring with them the number of average investors they have in the company now and the number of average investors they hope to entice into the company by a reduction in the price of the shares. I believe it is common knowledge that this is not a speculative company. It is a transportation company in the sense that it transports oil from western Canada to some parts of eastern Canada and the United States. There is no speculation in the business other than the volume handled from year to year. This figure has remained relatively stable, with an increase each year. Before six o'clock I should like to pose a number of questions so that the company can come to the Committee and give the answers. They should tell us what they hope to achieve by the co-operation of the average Canadian investor. Share splitting will certainly enhance their own position with the shareholders but how will they enhance the position of the average Canadian investor by this method?
It is my understanding, Mr. Speaker, that the bill will be sent to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines. On that understanding I will conclude my remarks.
Question, question.
Six o'clock.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 8 p.m.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Bell:
That this House recognizes the need for improving its procedures to provide full opportunity for the critical examination of proposed legislation and to ensure the effective dispatch of public business:
That this House agrees upon the need for allocating the time for the business of the House; and
That, in order to secure improved examination of the details of legislation and of public spending, while maintaining the full authority of the House, this House agrees upon the value of making increased use of Standing Committees;
That this House accordingly orders;
1.	(a) That detailed examination of estimates, saving always the right of the Committee of Supply, be undertaken by Standing Committees and that not more than 30 days of the time of the House be allocated to the business of supply in each session. For the purpose of this order, the business of supply shall consist of main estimates; interim supply; and supplementary or additional estimates excepting supplementary or additional estimates introduced after the main estimates have been approved, and excepting always the final supplementary or additional estimates;
(b)	That the number of supply motions be reduced from six to four; and
(c)	That a Special Committee of the House, consisting of twenty-four members, to be designated later by the House, be instructed to prepare and to submit to the House forthwith the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon these orders, including any means of giving to the opposition an opportunity to select the departmental estimates to be discussed.
2.	That the Standing Orders be amended by adding thereto a new Standing Order 15-A, to read as follows:
Standing Order 15-A
15-A. (1) There shall be a Business Committee to which the leader of each party in the House from time to time by written notice to the Speaker may appoint one member.
(2)	During routine proceedings a Minister of the Crown may request that the question of allocation of time for consideration of any item of business or stage thereof be referred to the Business Committee for consideration and report, and upon such request being made such question shall stand referred to the committee.
(3)	The Business Committee shall report back to the House on or before the third sitting day following such request.
(4)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the Committee has unanimously recommended an allocation of time for the item of business or stage thereof, a Minister of the Crown may without notice propose a motion to be decided without debate or amendment, for concurrence in the report, and, if agreed to, the motion shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(5)	If the Chairman of the Business Committee reports that the committee has been unable to reach a unanimous agreement or if the committee fails to report within the time specified by Section (3) of this Standing Order, a Minister of the Crown may give notice that at the next sitting of the House he will move that an order be made allocating the time for the item of business or stage thereof.
(6)	A motion of which a Minister has given notice under Section (5) of this Standing Order shall be made during routine proceedings. Unless the debate on the motion has been previously concluded, Mr. Speaker shall at fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for Government business in such sitting, interrupt the proceedings and forthwith put every question necessary to dispose of the main motion. A motion requesting allocation of time, if agreed to, shall have the same effect as if it were an order of the House.
(7)	No motion made by a Minister under Sections (5) and (6) of this Standing Order shall provide for the allocation of a period of time shorter than two days for the second reading, two days for the committee stage, and one day for the third reading of any bill. For the purposes of this section, third reading shall be deemed to have been considered for one day provided the order for third reading is called as the first item under Government Orders on a Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, and provided it is continued, il necessary, until the normal time of adjournment on any such day; provided that if a representative of each party has not spoken, the hour for the adjournment of the sitting shall be extended until a representative of each party has had an opportunity to speak. Such an order having been called on any Monday, Tuesday, Thursday or Friday, it shall have precedence over all other business until the time of adjournment on that
2122	COMMONS
House of Commons Procedures day, unless it is disposed of earlier. Under any other circumstances, a total of five hours shall be deemed to be the equivalent of one sitting day.
(8)	During debate on any item of business or stage thereof for which an allocation of time has been made under this Standing Order, if an amendment is proposed which in the opinion of Mr. Speaker materially changes the item of business or stage thereof and which raises any issue for which in the opinion of Mr. Speaker there has not been or otherwise will not be an adequate opportunity for discussion, Mr. Speaker may announce an extension of not more than two days to the allocated period of time.
(9)	The term "allocation of time", wherever used in this Standing Order, may include the allotting of time to any item of business, to any stage thereof, or to any part thereof, and may include the fixing of limits for the length of speeches.
3.	That the orders of this House under numbered paragraph 1, the changes in Standing Orders consequential upon these Orders, and the new Standing Order 15A be continued in effect until the end of the next ensuing session, unless this House otherwise orders.
